(a) Study by GAO.—The Comptroller General of the United States shall conduct a study to determine the following:
        (1) The rate of first cycle approvals and tentative approvals for applications submitted under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 355(j)) during the period beginning on October 1, 2012, and ending on September 30, 2017. The rate of first cycle approvals and tentative approvals shall be determined and reported per each GDUFA cohort year during this period. 
        (2) If the rate determined pursuant to paragraph (1) for any GDUFA cohort year is lower than 20 percent, the reasons contributing to the relatively low rate of first cycle approvals and tentative approvals for generic drug applications shall be itemized, assessed, and reported. In making the assessment required by this paragraph, the Comptroller General shall consider, among other things, the role played by—
            (A) the Food and Drug Administration’s implementation of approval standards for generic drug applications; 
            (B) the extent to which those approval standards are communicated clearly to industry and applied consistently during the review process; 
            (C) the procedures for reviewing generic drug applications, including timelines for review activities by the Food and Drug Administration; 
            (D) the extent to which those procedures are followed consistently (and those timelines are met) by the Food and Drug Administration; 
            (E) the processes and practices for communication between the Food and Drug Administration and sponsors of generic drug applications; and 
            (F) the completeness and quality of original generic drug applications submitted to the Food and Drug Administration.  
        (3) Taking into account the determinations made pursuant to paragraphs (1) and (2) and any review process improvements implemented pursuant to this Act, whether there are ways the review process for generic drugs could be improved to increase the rate of first cycle approvals and tentative approvals for generic drug applications. In making this determination, the Comptroller General shall consider, among other things, options for increasing review efficiency and communication effectiveness.  
    (b) Completion Date.—Not later than the expiration of the 2-year period beginning on the date of enactment of this Act, the Comptroller General shall complete the study under subsection (a) and submit a report describing the findings and conclusions of the study to the Secretary, the Committee on Energy and Commerce of the House of Representatives, and the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions of the Senate. 
    (c) Definitions.—For purposes of this section:
        (1) The term “GDUFA cohort year” means a fiscal year. 
        (2) The term “generic drug” means a drug that is approved or is seeking approval under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 355(j)). 
        (3) The term “generic drug application” means an abbreviated new drug application for the approval of a generic drug under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 355(j)). 
        (4) The term “Secretary” means the Secretary of Health and Human Services. 
        (5)
            (A) The term “first cycle approvals and tentative approvals” means the approval or tentative approval of a generic drug application after the Food and Drug Administration’s complete review of the application and without issuance of one or more complete response letters. 
            (B) For purposes of this paragraph, the term “complete response letter” means a written communication to the sponsor of a generic drug application or holder of a drug master file from the Food and Drug Administration describing all of the deficiencies that the Administration has identified in the generic drug application (including pending amendments) or drug master file that must be satisfactorily addressed before the generic drug application can be approved.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that references to communication with "industry" and "sponsors of generic drug applications" signal outside participation. Those are only topics the Comptroller General must assess in a GAO study, not a requirement to consult outside parties before a federal decision. The only procedural step is a report to the Secretary and congressional committees, all of whom are inside the federal government. Drug applications are also excluded as applications for approval.
fable.s: the Comptroller General shall complete the study under subsection (a) and submit a report describing the findings and conclusions of the study to the Secretary, the Committee on Energy and Commerce of the House of Representatives, and the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions of the Senate.

qwen_block.w: This section mandates a study by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), which is an internal federal agency, and requires the submission of a report to other federal entities (the Secretary of HHS and Congressional committees). There is no requirement for consultation with or participation by outside parties (such as the public, industry, or states) in the decision-making process. The mention of 'industry' in subsection (a)(2)(B) refers to how FDA standards are communicated to them, not to a participatory process involving them in the study itself.
qwen_block.s: The Comptroller General of the United States shall conduct a study to determine the following... submit a report describing the findings and conclusions of the study to the Secretary, the Committee on Energy and Commerce of the House of Representatives, and the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions of the Senate.

opus.w: The section tells the Comptroller General to conduct a study and report to the HHS Secretary and to congressional committees, all of whom are inside the federal government. Industry and drug sponsors appear only as subjects of the study, not as people consulted before a federal decision. There is no comment period, hearing, advisory panel, or right to sue. As in the GAO-style study examples, a report to Congress does not count as participation.
opus.s: the Comptroller General shall complete the study under subsection (a) and submit a report describing the findings and conclusions of the study to the Secretary, the Committee on Energy and Commerce of the House of Representatives, and the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions of the Senate.
opus.b: The tempting reading is that this section involves outside parties, since it talks about "communication between the Food and Drug Administration and sponsors of generic drug applications" and approval standards "communicated clearly to industry." That reading fails because these are only topics the GAO must study. They do not create any process for outsiders to take part in a federal decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section mandates a study by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), which is an internal federal agency. The study is to be reported to the Secretary of Health and Human Services and congressional committees, all of which are inside the federal government. While the study analyzes communication with industry sponsors, it does not require the government to consult with or coordinate with outside parties before making a decision. It is an internal review process.

qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the study considers "communication between the Food and Drug Administration and sponsors of generic drug applications" (subsection (a)(2)(E)), it involves participation. However, this is merely a subject of analysis for a government study, not a requirement for the sponsors to participate in a decision-making process. The study itself is conducted by the GAO (an internal government entity) and reported to Congress and the Secretary (internal government entities). There is no requirement for public comment, consultation with outside parties before a decision, or an advisory board with outside members. The "sponsors" are applicants for regulatory approval, and their interaction is part of the application review process, not "participation" as defined (which excludes applications for benefits/grants/licenses and requires consultation/coordination *before* a decision by the government involving outsiders). The definition explicitly states: "It does not include applications for benefits or grants." While this is a study, not an application, the interaction described is retrospective analysis of existing processes, not a mandated participatory mechanism for future decisions.
